en: Title: *Deśanāstava* (The Praise of Confession) Author: Candragomin Source: Liu & Schneider 2022, pp. 55–62
Tibetan: D 1159; see Tatz 1978, Hahn 1993, 2016. Input: Péter-Dániel Szántó, 18/07/2025. % p. 55
Homage to the Buddha.

Having approached you for refuge— you who are free from all faults, a mine of virtues, the teacher of the world, and the peerless King of Physicians— the one who is eternally afflicted [with disease]—
I confess my own faults and their transformations. || 1 ||
Like two rivers with currents difficult to cross, surging with waves of ill-considered reflections and discursive thoughts, and teeming with a multitude of crocodiles that are the afflictions.
Even in my own mind, there is no peace. || 2 ||
If I were to take refuge in the raft of the unattractive amidst the ocean of passion crowded with great waves,
it would burn him up there like a dry thicket.
The fire of hatred destroys my mind. || 3 ||
If I cultivate a mind of loving-kindness in order to pacify the torment of the fire of hatred,
then [I shall meditate upon] that which is cherished by the happiness of all beings.
The mind plunges into the mire of affection.
If I were to wash that [body], which is defiled by the mud of grease, for the sake of purification with indifference, then how could there be the attainment of the state of a Buddha,
which brings relief from the suffering of the entire world?
Even the compassion of the Lord of the World diminishes. || 5 ||
O Lord, if I cultivate compassion,
great weariness arises within me; if, for the sake of pacifying this, I resort to sympathetic joy—
The mind becomes agitated and fickle. || 6 ||
If one trembles for the sake of pacifying joy, the mind there becomes sluggish and despondent.
If, through exertion, one attains eminence,
it comes within the range of even those who are enemies of humanity.
Just as an enemy [is neutralized], all emptiness is stilled therein; yet, for the sake of others,
he maintains respect for conventional reality if he undertakes it for the benefit of others.
There the mind shines forth with the hope for wealth. || 8 ||
The mind has been diminished in its pursuit of acquiring wealth,
made to drink the intoxicant of all vices, and deluded by the sleep of the infatuation of pride.
And everything desired has indeed been destroyed. || 9 ||
Even when my mind desires to give, it is overcome by powerful stinginess; yet, if only that [stinginess] were shaken off, one would indeed give.
Then one repents for a long time. || 10 ||
If, moreover, that which has been purified by faith falls into the fruit pertaining to the next world,
it is rendered free from longing through the perception of impermanence.
Lacking signs and lacking effort, he suffers. || 11 ||
O Lord, although you observe that the world— though it has been a kinsman in all births— is tormented by extreme suffering,
you still strive for the sake of others.
It is devoured helplessly by the notion of a self.
Following the view of a self, the ego-sense creates the grasping of "mine";
therein arise pride, intoxication, passion, and the rest.
They afflict [us] like enraged enemies. || 13 ||
Then, the net of afflictions rose up on all sides like a terrifying army of Māra.
Then the night of the dark fortnight unfolds, terrible like the Night of Doom.
I know that evil is unbearable in its remorse and terrible in its transformation into suffering and rebirth; yet, I myself still commit it.
What indeed could be more painful than this? (15)
If the mind, which is the cause of manifold sufferings, has been restrained from harming others,
it is nevertheless agitated by the harshness of sword-leaves.
By wicked people who are enemies without having caused any offense. || 16 ||
Even when my mind desires to be patient, it is bound by the fetters of resentment; therefore,
it is agitated and concentrated upon that very suppression.
Harsh with the complete parching of the fire of hatred. || 17 ||
Just as birds avoid a tree whose hollows are infested with the venom of fierce-looking serpents,
so too do they avoid one who conceals the transformation of their resentment.
The wise avoid my intention. || 18 ||
Like a stone scorched by the rays of the sun,
like parched and dusty ashes,
or like a path thick with sand and clouds of dust.
The rain of Dharma has been fruitless within my heart.
He who, disregarding his own terrible suffering, has exerted himself as if for my own benefit— this supreme benefactor of patience and generosity—
O Lord of the World, I cannot endure even that. || 20 ||
Even while being hostile, fleeing, quivering, or causing pain, [he remains so].
Such a person as he instructs me incessantly, yet he does not appear to me as a teacher.
Having attained that which is difficult to find and worthy of prayer—
the supreme great festival of obtaining patience—
if, despite possessing the virtue of patience, I am not patient; [then what is the point?]
What other cause for patience do I have?
Beholding the world seized by the rākṣasa of the afflictions, agitated, feverish, disregarding its own welfare, and incapable of looking [toward liberation], [the Bodhisattva...]
O Lord, my very hatred is compassion for you. || 23 ||
I know that all people are the recipients of the fruits of their own actions, helpless and perishable;
yet I imagine another to be the perpetrator of the offense.
Behold the manifestation of the darkness of delusion! || 24 ||
I am an ocean of faults, O Lord, and I cannot endure even a fraction of a fault in anyone else,
since I am unable to forgive even the abundance of others' virtues.
I cannot endure this supreme wonder.
Like masses of clouds rising on all sides during the rainy season, the multitudes of afflictions repeatedly bring about a gathering within my mind.
Fie on waters that are sluggish once they have abandoned their flow! 26.
I am resolved to conquer by means of meditative concentration the web of afflictions that has arisen,
should the darkness of sloth and torpor manifest.
And the longing for beds and seats increases. || 27 ||
The mind is rendered helpless by the noose of passion,
consumed by hatred, and shattered by pride.
Being struck on all sides by the arrows, spears, and javelins of all the faults, it becomes utterly bewildered. || 28 ||
Having gained consciousness, it remains bound;
it trembles, is repelled, and desponds,
deceived by illusion and deceit.
He wanders bewildered within the domain of Māra. || 29 ||
Whatever the object of calm abiding may be, wherever the mind is repeatedly directed toward it,
it is no longer rendered helpless by the snares of the afflictions.
He is dragged away by the ropes of greed for sense-objects. || 30 ||
It brings forth energy that has arisen, and it abandons that which has become agitated; thus, lethargy arises.
For such a person, the state of being endowed with balanced application is difficult to attain.
What can my agitated mind do? || 31 ||
If one practices with wisdom, there arises agitation;
if one resorts to concentration, there arises dullness.
For such a person, the state of the yoked pair (yuganaddha) is difficult to attain.
What can my agitated mind do? || 32 ||
If one exerts effort toward what has arisen in an excited state, it becomes softened; if one does not, laxity arises.
This middle way is difficult to attain.
What can my agitated mind do? || 33 ||
Though the forest of faults is repeatedly scorched by the forest fires of meditative concentration,
its firm root— the view of a self— remains firmly planted.
It sprouts forth on all sides, as if during the rainy season. || 34 ||
Even though that [continuum] ceases for one who perceives the continuum as consisting merely of afflictions, karma, and its fruit;
Even the continuum of the mind is abandoned; how much more so the exertion for the sake of the world! (35)
The mental continuum of a yogi who is devoid of even a trace of affection and who proceeds with indifference toward all sentient beings attains extinction.
Like the continuity of a lamp [extinguished] through the exhaustion of its fuel. || 36 ||
The thought of awakening is nectar, an elixir that destroys the suffering of the entire world;
it is the cause of enlightenment, cultivated through non-conceptualization.
In that regard, it is only conceptual construction that runs for me. || 37 ||
Even while contemplating that nothing at all in this world can be grasped by anyone, as if it were a dream-form, I move within the range of sensory experience.
[He is] the enemy of the conceptual constructions of the object of awakening and the subject who awakens. || 38 ||
O Lord, bestow upon me your stainless gaze; behold this most terrible slaughter,
wherein my very conception of essence resides.
That very thing dissolves right before one's eyes. || 39 ||
What can the Blessed One do here, or rather,
it is simply my own fault committed in a previous life;
for the sun is the dispeller of the darkness of the entire world.
It dispels blindness and the blinding darkness. || 40 ||
Of one who has indulged in long-term causes,
whose mind there is perpetually deluded,
and who is a leper with shriveled hands and feet.
What can a remedy do once it has been administered? || 41 ||
The tree of the mind, which has existed from beginningless time, is permeated by the watering of the bitter flavor of the afflictions.
Can drops of water, even if they possess qualities, ever be capable of bringing sweetness to [something already sweet]? || 42 ||
My mind, though consisting entirely of all defects, has become a marvelous elixir of gold that is awakening;
it is precisely those very same qualities that have been bestowed upon it.
Having brought about the state of being a fault, it remains. || 43 ||
Whatever great medicine is prescribed, that very thing turns into poison within me;
for reason alone is the supreme elixir.
And that [cessation] does not exist; if it does not exist, there is no liberation. || 44 ||
But that which burns away the fullness of the faults,
yet does not provoke another fault— that,
I believe, is the correct method.
"What kind [it is]"—there is no further determination. || 45 ||

For those who meditate upon the cultivation of that instruction, [which removes] the latent tendencies of intention and underlying dispositions, the impressions of the elements, and the application of causes for faults that are contrary [to reality].
Peace will come here before long. || 46 ||
For you, the Protector who is free from all faults and who knows the ultimate truth of all phenomena,
even your form, though variegated, has been defined as formless.
It removes all the impurities of the defects. || 47 ||
Furthermore, for those beholding this form standing before you, radiant with beautiful marks,
it is like nectar to be drunk by the ears for those who hear it.
The entire web of afflictions is shattered. || 48 ||
Furthermore, O Lord, that unsurpassed sun of the Dharmakāya which is even beyond that—
Even when merely contemplated, it brings about the non-arising of the world and destroys darkness; that indeed is wonderful.
Established in tranquility wherever it may be, with whatever supreme mind one possesses,
one should act in such a way as to bring happiness to the entire world.
Whoever you may be, O Blessed One, homage be to you! || 50 ||
Before you, who are free from all defects, I, whose self is defiled by every fault,
have confessed my own impurity and the accumulation of my sins.
You are the teacher of the world; beyond this, you are the Lord.
By whatever merit has been acquired by me here, may [all beings], endowed with the glory of victory over Māra,
attain the path consisting of meditative cultivation.
May embodied beings attain the awakening of a Buddha. || 52 ||
The *Deśanāstava* is completed.
This is the work of the venerable Candragomin.
